title: Worldbuilding possibility map
authorship: AI synthesis of the archived conversation, selected earlier project sources, and dated evidence notes. All node descriptions, classifications, links, and inferences are AI-written proposals, not verbatim quotations from Ren. Source records distinguish founder theses, assistant interpretation, and bounded reviews of primary operational evidence.
purpose: A revisable typed network connecting a concrete engineering program for expanding productive capacity to generous shared provision, freedom from compulsory employment, and generative worldmaking. It links principles, scenario premises, mechanisms, conditional expectations, worlds, tensions, and open technical questions. It is not an inevitability tree or a dated forecast.
evidence_policy: Sources S1–S8 and S12 establish conversational or historical provenance; S13 records authorization to prepare the next edition and update the project, not new philosophical claims or acceptance of particular designs; S9 is an assistant-authored source-reading record. S10–S11 are dated, bounded assistant reviews of linked primary operational and research reports, with their reported scopes and limitations. Evidence for a component, local deployment, or useful feedback link does not establish full autonomous industrial reproduction, current-model sufficiency for every required task, an expansion timetable, or a guaranteed institutional outcome. Preserve Ren’s strong engineering thesis explicitly and test it at the declared network scale; do not silently promote the thesis or a scenario premise to a demonstrated fact.
path_base: All source paths and artifact paths are relative to this JSON file.

node_types.principle: A normative commitment: what this civilization should protect or pursue.
node_types.assumption: A scenario premise requiring evidence before it can support a claim about the actual world.
node_types.mechanism: A proposed institutional or design arrangement with effects to examine.
node_types.expectation: A conditional hypothesis about behavior or social outcomes, open to failure.
node_types.world: A concrete speculative setting or explicitly unexpanded seed.
node_types.tension: A risk, limit, conflict, or tradeoff that must remain visible.
node_types.question: An unresolved inquiry that can generate research or design work.

relation_semantics.requires: Source is conditional on target within this scenario. The target is not claimed to be sufficient; this is not universal logical necessity.
relation_semantics.supports: Source offers a reason, enabling condition, or proposed contribution toward target. It does not establish target or guarantee its outcome.
relation_semantics.constrains: Source sets a design boundary, feasibility limit, or countervailing pressure on target. Normative constraints must be institutionally implemented.
relation_semantics.tests: Source world supplies a fictional design test of target. A scene or simulation can expose incoherence but is not empirical validation.
relation_semantics.risks: Source creates or encounters exposure to target failure mode. Neither a probability nor inevitability is asserted.
relation_semantics.mitigates: Source proposes a way to reduce target risk. Effectiveness and secondary effects remain to be examined.
relation_semantics.asks_about: Source question directs inquiry toward target.

conventions: IDs remain stable when prose is refined. Do not renumber surviving nodes; record replacement IDs if a node is split or retired.
An arrow follows source to target and means only its named relation; read the relation before following a path.
No transitive inference is licensed automatically. Supports plus supports does not establish an outcome.
Values do not manufacture technical capability. Principle-to-mechanism links concern design intent, not engineering proof.
Cycles may represent mutual support or revision. The map is not restricted to a tree or a directed acyclic graph.
Missing edges do not establish independence. The map is intentionally selective, and scope should be expanded where a scenario needs it.
No probabilities, universal growth rates, calendar predictions, or final institutional settlement are assigned.

nodes.title: Unconditional belonging
nodes.description: A person’s material security and standing do not depend on employment, competitive success, prestige, or being judged sufficiently generative.

nodes.title: Care for the shared substrate
nodes.description: Communities share ecological and material conditions. Their projects must account for effects on other people, other living systems, and future inhabitants.

nodes.title: Plural ways of being
nodes.description: A shared civilization can hold scholarly, expressive, exploratory, quiet, and mixed lives. Belonging does not require one account of a good life.

nodes.title: Generative ambition without compulsory productivity
nodes.description: Culture can encourage creating possibilities beyond oneself while protecting rest, ordinary affection, unremarkable lives, and the freedom to stop.

nodes.title: Consent, refusal, and exit
nodes.description: People can refuse personalization, criticize institutions, leave communities, and retain material security. Others’ attention, affection, and agreement remain voluntary.

nodes.title: Competition with bounded consequences
nodes.description: Games and rivalry can be intense, but winning must not determine access to essentials or transfer authority over shared life-support systems.

nodes.title: Learning as a way of inhabiting reality
nodes.description: Understanding, embodied practice, expression, and exploration can be valued for how they change experience, beyond their usefulness for employment.

nodes.title: Revisable shared governance
nodes.description: Institutions must be open to criticism and repair, with intelligible decisions and ways to challenge or replace administrators. No single vision is beyond revision.

nodes.title: Reliable autonomy across required tasks
nodes.description: Ren’s engineering thesis is that present AI methods and industrial knowledge can be developed into full automation. The strong scenario grants adequate reliability and recoverability across the cognitive and physical tasks required for infrastructure and everyday provision. Bounded operating capabilities make this a concrete program to pursue, but do not establish that today’s available models are sufficient for every required task.
validation_needed: Specify required tasks and operating conditions.
Assess failures, repair needs, supervision, and dependence on scarce human expertise.
nodes.evidence_context: The two dated evidence notes report useful operating pieces and development methods. Q09 asks whether the actual required task network can be completed with current systems; A01 remains unverified at universal scope.

nodes.title: Industrial reproduction with supply-chain closure
nodes.description: The strong scenario grants a productive network able to construct, commission, maintain, and reproduce its required equipment, including upstream tools and critical components within a declared boundary. A robot factory alone does not establish this closure. Useful recursive expansion within an externally supplied network is a less demanding route, represented separately by M14.
validation_needed: Trace energy, extraction, refining, chips, machine tools, transport, construction, maintenance, and waste streams.
Identify dependencies the proposed system cannot itself replenish.

nodes.title: Resource and energy access
nodes.description: Material inputs, usable energy, suitable sites, logistics, and lawful access are available at the scale required by the selected scenario. These are finite and spatially uneven.
validation_needed: Build material and energy budgets for a chosen scale.
Identify lead times, contested access, and capacity constraints.

nodes.title: Growth through reinvested productive capacity
nodes.description: In the strong industrial-closure scenario, output reinvested in further useful capacity may accelerate expansion while complementary inputs, system closure, repairs, and commissioning keep pace. Positive net addition proportional to operating capacity would yield an exponential phase under those model conditions; this is not a measured industrial rate, universal doubling time, or indefinite planetary trajectory. M14 also explores recursive expansion with declared outside dependencies.
validation_needed: Define what grows: robot count, useful output, or complete productive capacity.
Model construction and commissioning delays, depreciation, reinvestment, and the slowest required input.

nodes.title: Provision within ecological limits
nodes.description: The chosen level of provision and construction can operate inside explicitly chosen ecological budgets, including material throughput, land use, waste, habitat effects, and energy infrastructure.
validation_needed: Define the budgets and how breaches are detected.
Compare maintenance, reuse, and restoration with new construction.

nodes.title: Durable provision and creation entitlement
nodes.description: Establish an enforceable, portable claim to dependable provision and an accessible share of tools or productive capacity. Essentials are a necessary guarantee within a larger aim of generous common means and creative freedom; the delivery and allocation model remains open, and access does not depend on selling labor.

nodes.title: Accountable stewardship of automated infrastructure
nodes.description: Choose ownership, operating mandates, audits, maintenance duties, and succession arrangements that preserve the provision guarantee and prevent operators from making residents dependent on their favor. No single ownership form is assumed to suffice.

nodes.title: Participatory allocation and appeal
nodes.description: Make decisions over shared space and rival resources through understandable procedures with representation, appeals, and protection for dissenting or less influential inhabitants.

nodes.title: Reversible trials and collective repair
nodes.description: Prototype changes where feasible, keep rollback and repair capacity, include affected people, and evaluate consequences before committing to larger transformations. Some ecological and social changes cannot be fully reversed.

nodes.title: Responsive environments under resident control
nodes.description: Buildings, gardens, mobility, and mixed-reality spaces can adapt to inhabitants, with intelligible controls, consent, physical accessibility, privacy, manual alternatives, and protected unpersonalized spaces.

nodes.title: Lifelong learning and practice commons
nodes.description: Make equipment, mentorship, spaces, knowledge, and time accessible across ages; support embodied and expressive practices alongside formal inquiry, and make leaving or returning ordinary.

nodes.title: Livelihood can separate from paid employment
nodes.description: If dependable provision requires much less human effort, remaining necessary work has acceptable arrangements, and people have durable common access, livelihood can separate from compulsory paid employment. The aim includes a generous life and usable means of creation. Reducing a task’s labor requirement alone does not grant its former workers access to the output, and one group’s freedom cannot hide another group’s coerced labor.
nodes.observation: Can inhabitants lose paid work or leave a community without losing housing, food, care, mobility, or access to tools?
nodes.challenge: Exclusion, administrator discretion, supply interruption, or unaffordable essentials continue to make livelihood conditional on labor or allegiance.

nodes.title: Lives may organize around diverse pursuits
nodes.description: With secure belonging and voluntary associations, more people may organize life around relationships, gardening, expression, inquiry, exploration, play, or rest. This is neither a prediction that everyone becomes a builder nor an obligation to do so.
nodes.observation: Do varied ways of life remain accessible, including changing interests and lives with little visible output?
nodes.challenge: Prestige hierarchies, exclusion, cultural pressure, or concentrated control make one approved way of life practically compulsory.

nodes.title: Physical speed can coexist with civic patience
nodes.description: If construction becomes faster, communities may choose to spend more time understanding consequences, relationships, memory, and consent before changing a place. Faster capability need not dictate faster collective decisions.
nodes.observation: Can residents delay, revise, or refuse a technically ready project without losing standing?
nodes.challenge: Output targets or operator power make consent ceremonial and erase places faster than inhabitants can respond.

nodes.title: Learning may become less credential-driven
nodes.description: When livelihoods are secure and learning resources are accessible, learning can increasingly follow curiosity, relationships, practice, and long commitments. Credentials may remain useful for responsibility and trusted expertise.
nodes.observation: Can someone study, stop, change fields, or practice privately without losing essentials or belonging?
nodes.challenge: Status competition recreates credential races, or access to respected mentors and equipment remains restricted.

nodes.title: Living garden
nodes.description: A neighborhood shaped around habitat, food, seasons, shared space, and ecological stewardship. A proposed resident changes from garden planning to astronomy while retaining ordinary provision and creative means; an affected group revises a building footprint to keep a mature tree. These scenes examine durable access, remaining human work, ecological continuity, and whose preferred landscape becomes real.

nodes.title: House of worlds
nodes.description: A megastructure purpose-built for shared embodied AR, where world halls, portal lifts, touchable routes, and service levels support persistent collectively authored realities. The current concept uses three broad stacked halls, a left passenger core, a right service core, and a cloud-harbor music gathering called the First Arrival. Dedicated AR purpose is Ren’s direction; this geometry, culture, and display approach remain proposals. Shared physics, accessible exits, and support spaces remain real.
nodes.user_direction: A mega building built for AR purposes, as clarified in S12. Earlier treatment as an ordinary mixed-use building with added experiences is superseded.

nodes.title: Open university
nodes.description: An inhabited learning commons that welcomes lifelong inquiry, making, teaching, departure, and return. It must make room for varied abilities and nonacademic lives without treating membership as a rank.

nodes.title: Expressive commons
nodes.description: A community organized around movement, music, feeling, performance, and embodied exploration, with quiet rooms, privacy, and ordinary rest as complete ways to belong. Its proposed culture lets participants revise invitations and performance space without making participation, talent, or emotional disclosure a condition of security. A music room also explores the assessed reuse of a former garden pavilion’s structural bay.

nodes.title: Exploration community
nodes.description: A community that makes exploration a shared way of life: robotic fabrication, rocket and spacecraft work, observatories, long missions, and public learning support projects that outlast participants. The scenario separates workshops and public life from hazardous launch operations. Specific vehicles, destinations, and mission claims require their own feasibility cases.

nodes.title: Ownership and operator capture
nodes.description: High productive capacity may coexist with dependence if a few actors can deny access, set conditions, or monopolize infrastructure. Abundance and widely shared security are separate claims.

nodes.title: Ecological overshoot and displaced harm
nodes.description: Cheap or rapid construction may increase total material use, occupy habitats, move pollution elsewhere, or consume resources needed by other communities and future inhabitants.

nodes.title: Incomplete closure and scaling bottlenecks
nodes.description: A missing upstream capability, limited energy, scarce components, long lead times, maintenance burden, or repair failure can stop expansion or reduce provision. Scaling may be local, uneven, or stalled.

nodes.title: Scarce attention, place, and prestige
nodes.description: Affection, trust, recognition, unique places, and some opportunities remain rival or voluntary. Informal rankings can become coercive and unequal influence can survive material abundance.

nodes.title: Paternalistic or manipulative environments
nodes.description: A responsive system or institution may shape inhabitants toward its preferred behavior, make choices illegible, normalize surveillance, or penalize refusal while claiming to help.

nodes.title: Inherited habits and disrupted identity
nodes.description: People may experience guilt about rest, loss of identity, distrust of security, or pressure to prove usefulness. Different generations and cultures may inhabit the change differently.

nodes.title: How are rival goods allocated?
nodes.description: How should communities allocate unique places, scarce equipment time, ecological capacity, and opportunities without converting prestige or administrative favor into a right to dominate?

nodes.title: How do different worlds coexist?
nodes.description: How can communities with incompatible rhythms, landscapes, experiences, or projects share infrastructure and ecological budgets while preserving criticism, exit, and minority ways of life?

nodes.title: What makes a productive system dependable?
nodes.description: What operating evidence would justify granting autonomy and industrial closure at a particular scale, and what fallback provision remains available through failures, repair periods, or stalled expansion?

nodes.title: How do guarantees survive institutional failure?
nodes.description: Who enforces provision and access when owners, operators, communities, or governing bodies fail, and how can people replace them without interrupting essential services?

nodes.title: Long-horizon regenerative stewardship
nodes.description: Treat materials, ecosystems, and productive infrastructure as inheritances to care for across generations. Favor durable service, repair, recoverable transformation, and ecological restoration over repeated extraction and disposal; circulating objects alone does not establish regeneration.

nodes.title: Knowledge as a shared foundation
nodes.description: Develop knowledge, repair documentation, design records, and understandable standards as accessible public goods so people can learn, inspect, adapt, and build together. Public information does not by itself confer physical access or establish the performance of a manufactured object.

nodes.title: Recoverable material flows with usable energy and access
nodes.description: For the selected objects and places, collection, cleaning, inspection, sorting, repair, remanufacture, and recycling recover enough usable material to sustain the intended service, with accessible facilities, logistics, reserves, and energy. Recovery is specified by material and application; neither lossless cycles nor energy without environmental cost is assumed.
validation_needed: Specify the service, material grades, stock in use, return rate, retention of quality, processing losses, and unavoidable replacement inputs.
Account for cleaning, collection distances, storage, inspection, repair, manufacturing energy, water, residues, and access to facilities.
Test whether reserve stock and recovery throughput maintain provision through demand changes, outages, and delayed returns.

nodes.title: Shared durable services and return loops
nodes.description: Provide functions through durable objects and convenient return, cleaning, repair, and redistribution systems where a whole-system comparison supports them. A shared metal cup is a starting design case; personal use and long possession remain possible, and the loop must work for different bodies, preferences, and daily rhythms.

nodes.title: Compatible repairable parts and open standards
nodes.description: Develop interoperable interfaces, replaceable parts, identified material grades, repair instructions, and revisable open standards. Choose fabrication methods for the application, including 3D printing where suitable; a shared design file does not establish material quality, dimensional accuracy, or structural fitness.

nodes.title: Architecture designed for disassembly and reuse
nodes.description: Design structures and fit-outs with accessible reversible connections, identifiable components, documented histories, and safe disassembly routes. Robots may assemble and recover steel members or other suitable parts; each reuse requires condition assessment and a design-specific performance case. Material reversibility does not reverse every ecological or social consequence.

nodes.title: Material inventory and recovery reserves
nodes.description: Maintain an intelligible record of material quantities, grades, condition, location, commitments, and routes for return, alongside reserves for repair and interrupted processing. Use this information to match available parts to new purposes and expose losses and bottlenecks without making personal tracking a condition of access.

nodes.title: Freedom through recoverable reconfiguration
nodes.description: With usable recovery systems, compatible parts, accessible knowledge, and legitimate decisions, people may gain freedom to revise their surroundings while retaining more of the material capacity for later uses. A finite circulating stock can support repeated reconfiguration within quality and throughput limits; expanding simultaneous buildings or factories still requires stock, energy, space, and capacity.
nodes.observation: Can a community change a useful space, recover and redeploy its components, and retain dependable provision while recording losses, energy, elapsed time, and affected residents’ choices?
nodes.challenge: Frequent redesign consumes the recovery margin, compatible parts become inaccessible, or the ability to change places faster erodes continuity and consent.

nodes.title: Material quality, losses, and recovery bottlenecks
nodes.description: Collection failures, dispersed materials, incompatible mixtures, wear, contamination, processing losses, stock tied up in long-lived objects, and limited recovery capacity can interrupt the intended loops. A high recycling claim by itself does not specify how much suitable material returns, when it becomes available, or what new inputs are still required.

nodes.title: Amplified harmful will and unnecessary churn
nodes.description: Powerful fabrication and rapid reconfiguration can amplify destructive intentions, unilateral redesign, status-driven novelty, and avoidable replacement. Even recoverable construction can consume energy, disrupt lives or habitats, and overwhelm repair and deliberation. The ability to act does not establish a right to impose the result.

nodes.title: How does finite circulating stock relate to growth?
nodes.description: For a chosen region and service level, distinguish more simultaneous productive capacity from more varied uses of existing stock. What additional stock, energy, throughput, replacement inputs, and ecological capacity does each require, and when should reinvested expansion slow, stop, or shift toward maintenance and reconfiguration?

nodes.title: When does collective provision improve the whole system?
nodes.description: Compared with durable personal provision, when does a shared service reduce total burdens while preserving convenience, autonomy, reliability, and access? Test actual use frequency, cleaning, travel, returns, reserves, loss, and user preferences rather than treating collective provision as automatically superior.

nodes.title: Sustain the conditions of continuing becoming
nodes.description: Cultivate a living environment in which relationships, practices, knowledge, and forms of life can emerge and develop while sustaining their shared foundations. Generativity concerns the capacity for further life and creation; it is neither a command to maximize a count of options nor a demand for constant novelty. Particular forms can mature, end, or be mourned.

nodes.title: Participate as a coauthor of shared conditions
nodes.description: Understand oneself as an interdependent participant whose choices help shape other lives and the world that shapes oneself. Take responsibility for the conditions a project creates beyond its owner, and make room for affected people to help author them. Interdependence does not erase personal boundaries or by itself settle what anyone ought to do.

nodes.title: Keep understanding revisable and give learning time
nodes.description: Treat models, principles, and narratives as useful but partial guides. Cultivate curiosity, embodied attention, comparison, criticism, and time to notice consequences as capabilities and environments change. Even this orientation can be questioned; it supplies neither a final doctrine nor a numerical law relating technological speed to human understanding.

nodes.title: Practices of reciprocal worldmaking
nodes.description: Develop shared meals, mentorship, care, artistic rituals, expeditions, and resident-authored projects through which people learn to notice dependencies, contribute to something beyond themselves, and welcome others into it. These practices make the culture tangible while leaving belonging independent of contribution and allowing communities to develop different traditions.

nodes.title: Shared imagination, lived trials, and cultural revision
nodes.description: Let inhabitants propose worlds and rituals, build inspectable representations, try changes at a suitable scale, and compare lived consequences with intentions. Use stories, discussion, observation, and accessible records to revise both arrangements and the ideas guiding them. Participants can dispute interpretations and choose continuity; permanent changes need their own judgment rather than a blanket reversibility test.

nodes.title: People and their environments may reshape one another
nodes.description: In a setting with participatory worldmaking, shared understandings may shape habits and expectations; these may shape choices, institutions, and material and social environments; experienced consequences may then revise or reinforce the original understandings. People can interpret the same world differently and change it in turn. This reciprocal formation is a working causal hypothesis with variable effects, not proof that one designed environment produces a particular kind of person.
nodes.observation: Across several projects, what do inhabitants notice, desire, reward, imitate, and imagine differently after living with their consequences? Include dissenting and unchanged experiences.
nodes.challenge: Effects are weak, imposed, uneven, or better explained by prior selection; the official story of cultural change differs from residents’ experience.

nodes.title: Shared projects may support meaning beyond personal victory
nodes.description: When people can freely join sustained, welcoming pursuits, some may find meaning in caring for a world, exploring together, or contributing to work that outlasts them. Relationships and ordinary life can carry the same depth. The scenario does not predict universal harmony, identical desires, or the disappearance of rivalry.
nodes.observation: Do people describe belonging, curiosity, care, play, or a shared future as reasons to remain, and can they change their involvement without loss of dignity?
nodes.challenge: Shared purpose becomes a loyalty test, labor obligation, prestige contest, or story used to conceal exploitation.

nodes.title: Compounding rewards can capture the rules of shared life
nodes.description: Where winning yields durable advantages that buy further victories or control over rules and necessities, feedback may concentrate power and teach people to organize increasingly around that contest. Powerful automation may amplify the mechanism. This is conditional on institutions, returns, and constraints; it is not a theorem that every competition converges to domination or that cooperation automatically avoids capture.

nodes.title: What ways of being do our worlds cultivate?
nodes.description: How do narratives, attention, habits, institutions, and physical experiences interact to shape what people can imagine and become? Examine what a shared project makes inviting, who helps author it, how it changes its authors, and whether its success sustains further life or increasingly channels everyone toward one form of winning.

nodes.title: City of shared quests
nodes.description: A lived world inspired by MMORPGs and LARP, with resident-authored districts, roles, quests, festivals, and persistent shared stories. A proposed guild observes that its success-based rule excludes newcomers from authorship, revises access, and examines what changes. This concerns creative participation, never a loss of necessities: the ordinary city and secure belonging remain available to residents who decline the fiction.

nodes.title: Connect available capabilities into dependable services
nodes.description: Compose learned perception, planning, tools, feedback, conventional controls, and suitable robots into repeatable useful services. Connect those services through explicit input and output requirements, maintenance, energy, logistics, and human support. Existing deployments provide starting components; measure reliability of the connected network rather than treating a set of demonstrations as a complete autonomous system.
nodes.evidence_context: The dated industrial and AI notes distinguish operating services, research demonstrations, reporting parties, and intervention limits. They support beginning integration and research, not certification of the entire network.

nodes.title: Reinvest output in complementary productive capacity
nodes.description: Direct part of useful output toward additional builders, production cells, power, tooling, logistics, and other processes that limit the next round of provision. Count commissioned additions and retirements, preserve maintenance capacity, and expose outside inputs. Additional builders can help create further builders before full supply-chain closure; whether net growth compounds depends on the whole chosen network.

nodes.title: Spread validated knowledge and learn from operation
nodes.description: Make design records, process improvements, failure lessons, and reusable robot skills available for adaptation across installations. Shared knowledge can reduce repeated discovery and improve existing equipment alongside hardware expansion. Preserve testing, local fit, consent for data use, and reliable records; copying a policy or drawing does not guarantee useful performance at another site.

nodes.title: Generous common provision and creative means
nodes.description: Build common services for good food, comfortable homes, care, hygiene, mobility, culture, and usable access to fabrication, instruments, materials, knowledge, and spaces for ambitious shared projects. Join dependable access to actual supply, maintenance, allocation, and coordination. The aspiration is a rich life and capacity to create beyond a subsistence floor, without promising unlimited quantities, one institutional form, or compulsory participation.

nodes.title: Provision may expand with less required human effort
nodes.description: If connected productive systems repeatedly complete useful services with less human effort per service, provision and further capacity may grow without a proportional increase in required human labor. Pairing this technical gain with dependable common access and acceptable arrangements for remaining work can support freedom from compulsory employment. Autonomous equipment counts alone do not measure the gain.
nodes.observation: Track complete useful service, quality, availability, human interventions, maintenance, upstream human effort, and newly commissioned capacity across several operating and replication cycles.
nodes.challenge: Human effort is shifted upstream, hidden in remote support, consumed by repair and commissioning, or grows as fast as service; access remains conditional on wages despite labor savings.

nodes.title: Abundant shared means can make voluntary worldmaking practicable
nodes.description: When generous provision, usable creative capacity, knowledge, stewardship, and coordination are available together, people may gather around rockets, gardens, scholarship, embodied worlds, or other long projects without needing those projects to earn their livelihoods. Free association can then lead to systems people can actually build and sustain. It remains a possible social outcome, not a guarantee from abundant machinery or an obligation to join a grand purpose.
nodes.observation: Can a new or unprestigious group obtain usable tools, materials, knowledge, and support for a viable noncommercial project, sustain it, share what it learns, and change its membership without jeopardizing anybody’s ordinary provision?
nodes.challenge: The common system supplies nominal entitlements without capacity, allocates creative means through prestige or allegiance, or leaves voluntary groups without maintenance and coordination.

nodes.title: What is the actual net growth of useful capacity?
nodes.description: For a specified network, how much output becomes additional commissioned capacity after maintenance, retirements, lead times, losses, and essential provision? Which complementary process limits the next cycle, which inputs remain external, and does useful capacity actually make subsequent additions faster? Establish the interval and stopping conditions of any compounding phase rather than inferring a doubling time from robot production alone.

nodes.title: Are current AI systems sufficient for the declared automation scope?
nodes.description: For a declared service and productive network, can available AI, conventional automation, and robots complete every required task under relevant conditions with adequate reliability, recovery, and acceptable human support? Separate integration work, environmental redesign, and improvements possible with existing methods from unresolved capability research. Test Ren’s strong current-knowledge thesis directly instead of asserting it proved or replacing it with a premise that ignores the construction program.

edges.rationale: Industrial closure assumes dependable autonomy in all tasks included in the closure boundary.

Within A04’s strongest closure scenario, complete productive systems must replenish upstream and maintenance dependencies as they grow. This does not claim that every useful local expansion requires full closure; M14 represents recursive capacity-building with declared outside inputs.
Expansion requires timely access to inputs, sites, energy, and logistics.
Any slow or missing dependency can cap growth, with no promised doubling time.
Reinvestment can amplify material throughput and land use as well as output.
Expansion must remain within the scenario’s ecological budgets; this is a normative scenario boundary, not a claim that ecosystems automatically enforce a safe stopping point.
Stewardship must account for wider and intergenerational consequences.
The entitlement is a proposed institutional expression of unconditional belonging, not a technical consequence of it.
Material claims must be portable and survive dissent, refusal, and exit.
Infrastructure control must be challengeable and revisable.
Winning contests or acquiring prestige must not grant control over provision.
Ownership and operating arrangements can make the guarantee durable; their existence alone does not ensure enforcement.
A dependable entitlement is necessary to translate capacity into freedom from wage dependence.
The fully automated version of this expectation presumes reliable task performance.

This dependency records the original strongest autonomous-provision scenario, which grants reproducible productive capacity. It is not a universal necessity for freedom from paid employment: M13–M16 and E08 explore useful provision with explicit outside supplies and remaining voluntary human work.
Provision depends on resource and energy access even without wages.
People need access to output; production totals alone do not confer security.
The entitlement needs durable implementation and accountable operation.
Concentrated discretionary access can defeat livelihood independence despite high output.
Interrupted provision can make security fragile even with formal rights.
Audits, enforceable duties, and replacement procedures may reduce capture but must themselves be evaluated.
Pluralism gives diverse pursuits legitimacy; actual freedom also needs access and security.
The imagined change must preserve rest and lives without visible achievements.
The strong version of this scenario presumes livelihoods are secure without employment.
